Closing with .f4 too early (moves 26. 29) slows the attack and hands White a free queenside race. Once the c-file is open, White’s queenside play can distract Black’s forces very quickly. That is the Family 4 squeeze.

notes.text: Pause and assess Look carefully before moving on. Black’s rooks sit on the only open file. Does that mean Black is fine? McShane thought so. He expected counterplay along the c-file. The catch: there are almost no entry squares. The file is open, but it does not invade. Teaching point: an open file only helps if your pieces can enter. Here White’s space and queenside majority matter more than Black’s temporary control of the file.

Lesson: activity that does not create threats is just noise.

notes.text: Black has captured on f5 with his pawn to prevent White from installing a powerful knight on e4. This gives rise to a generally complex position. Black may attempt to: I. Weaken White's kingside with. H7-h5-h4. 2. Transfer his queen and rook to the h-file with attacking chances. 3. Play. E5-e4 to open the h8-al diagonal and gain potential outposts on d3 and f3. As previously mentioned, White will often choose between playing f2-f3 or f2-f4. In this case the choice is relatively simple si nce.

notes.text: Takeaways 1. 21.bxc5 (instead of .Nxb5) is a serious alternative. Study that structure in the next chapter. 2. Owning the c-file meant little here. White’s space and queenside levers decided the game. 3. With nothing real on the queenside, Black must play for .f5. Closing with .f4 too early (moves 26. 29) slows the attack and hands White a free queenside race. Once the c-file is open, White’s queenside play can distract Black’s forces very quickly. That is the Family 4 squeeze.
